items.prompt: You're rewriting a technical update for a non-technical exec. Which of these is true audience awareness, and which crosses into something else?
choices: Telling the exec the fix will ship 'this week' when your real estimate is 'maybe next week' if it goes smoothly
Cutting the vendor rate-limit detail because it doesn't change what the exec needs to decide
Telling the peer engineer a rosier timeline than the manager, so they don't worry
Both A and C — adjusting the facts, not just the framing, for different audiences
items.explanation: Audience awareness changes what's foregrounded and how much detail is load-bearing — it never changes the underlying facts. Options A and C both alter the actual claim (timeline, honesty) between audiences, which is deception, not calibration, and it gets caught the moment two audiences compare notes.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'just tell the exec it's basically fixed' even though the fix hasn't shipped yet and could slip. What's the audience-aware response?
choices: Say it's fixed anyway — execs don't need the caveats
Say the fix is in progress with an expected ship date, and flag if that date is at real risk
Give the exec the same technical detail you'd give a peer, so they can judge the risk themselves
Avoid mentioning it until it's actually shipped
items.explanation: The exec doesn't need the technical detail, but they do need an accurate claim about status — 'in progress, expected [date]' is both scoped correctly and true. Saying 'basically fixed' when it isn't is the facts-changing failure mode, not simplification; staying silent until shipped denies them a decision-relevant fact (that a report was late) that they may hear about elsewhere first.

items.prompt: Why does BLUF (bottom line up front) matter more for an exec-level message than a peer-to-peer Slack message?
choices: Execs are less intelligent and need the conclusion spelled out
The medium is different, so grammar rules change
The exec reader has less time and context invested per message, so they need the ask/conclusion before deciding whether to keep reading
It doesn't actually matter more — BLUF is equally important everywhere
items.explanation: A peer already has shared context and is often continuing a conversation, so leading with detail before the point is low-cost. An exec reading many updates a day with no shared context will often stop reading before reaching a buried conclusion — putting the ask or bottom line first respects that their attention is the scarce resource, not their intelligence.

items.prompt: A message written with no specific audience in mind tends to default to which frame?
choices: A neutral, universally readable frame
The writer's own frame — typically the most technical, most detailed, least decision-oriented version
The most simplified possible version, to be safe
Whatever frame the previous message in the thread used
items.explanation: There's no such thing as a neutral default — without deliberately choosing a frame, a writer reverts to their own context and vocabulary, which is usually over-detailed for a manager and impenetrable for a non-technical exec. Audience awareness is the deliberate override of that default, not an occasional extra step.

items.prompt: A founder with a strong engineering background asks you a narrow technical question about the retry logic. Per the L3 failure modes, what should determine your answer's level of detail?
choices: Their title — always give executives the exec-summary version
What they're actually measured on and what they already know, regardless of title — here, they're asking a peer-level question and likely have peer-level context
Always default to the most simplified version to be safe with anyone senior
Match whatever level of detail they used in previous unrelated conversations
items.explanation: The lens is stake and existing context, not org-chart position. A founder asking a specific technical question is signaling they want the peer-level answer; defaulting to an exec summary because of their title would under-serve the actual question being asked — this is exactly the 'over-indexing on hierarchy instead of actual stake' failure mode from L3.

items.prompt: You send your manager a message that says 'just flagging that reconciliation was slow this week' with no further detail. What failure mode is this, per L3?
choices: Correct — managers prefer brief, low-detail updates
Skipping or burying the ask — the reader is left guessing whether anything is needed from them
This is fine as long as the facts are accurate
This is the exec-appropriate version, just sent to the wrong person
items.explanation: An ambiguous 'just flagging this' forces the reader to guess whether a response, decision, or action is expected — that's a failure of audience awareness even if every stated fact is true, because it doesn't answer the manager's real question ('does this threaten my commitments, and do you need something from me').
